description.en: Master min-heaps and max-heaps using Python's heapq module. Understand heap operations and build a priority queue.
description.ta: Python-ன் heapq module பயன்படுத்தி min-heaps மற்றும் max-heaps கற்றுக்கொள்ளுங்கள்.

story_variants.en:
## Vaathiyaar's Emergency Room

Vaathiyaar simulates a hospital ER. "The sickest patient is seen first — not the one who arrived first. That's a heap!"

### What is a Heap?
- A **complete binary tree** stored as an array
- **Min-heap**: Parent ≤ Children (smallest at root)
- **Max-heap**: Parent ≥ Children (largest at root)
- Insert and extract are both **O(log n)**
- Getting the min/max is **O(1)**

### Python's heapq Module

```python
import heapq

# Min-heap operations
nums = [5, 3, 8, 1, 2]
heapq.heapify(nums)        # Convert list to min-heap: O(n)
print(nums)                 # [1, 2, 8, 3, 5]

heapq.heappush(nums, 0)    # Insert 0: O(log n)
print(heapq.heappop(nums)) # Extract min (0): O(log n)

# Get k smallest/largest
data = [10, 4, 5, 8, 6, 11, 26]
print(heapq.nsmallest(3, data))  # [4, 5, 6]
print(heapq.nlargest(3, data))   # [26, 11, 10]
```

### Max-Heap Trick

```python
# Python only has min-heap, negate values for max-heap
max_heap = []
for val in [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]:
    heapq.heappush(max_heap, -val)

largest = -heapq.heappop(max_heap)  # 5
```

> **Key Concept:** Heaps are perfect for "top K" problems. Need the 3 largest? Use a min-heap of size 3!

animation_sequence.code:
import heapq

nums = [5, 3, 8, 1, 2]
heapq.heapify(nums)
print(f'Heapified: {nums}')

heapq.heappush(nums, 0)
print(f'After push 0: {nums}')

smallest = heapq.heappop(nums)
print(f'Popped min: {smallest}')

data = [10, 4, 5, 8, 6, 11, 26]
print(f'Top 3: {heapq.nlargest(3, data)}')
print(f'Bottom 3: {heapq.nsmallest(3, data)}')

executionSteps.explanation: Unsorted list — not yet a valid heap
heapify rearranges in O(n). Smallest (1) at index 0
Push 0 — bubbles up to root in O(log n)
heappop extracts min and restructures in O(log n)
nlargest uses heap internally — efficient for top-K

under_the_hood.summary: heapq keeps a plain list arranged so every parent is no larger than its children; push sifts the new item up and pop moves the last item to the root and sifts it down.

steps.title: A tree stored in a list
steps.body: A heap is a complete binary tree laid out level by level in an array. The node at index i has children at 2i+1 and 2i+2 and its parent at (i-1)//2. There are no node objects or pointers: [1, 2, 8, 5, 3] is a tree with 1 at the root, 2 and 8 below it, and 5 and 3 under the 2.

steps.title: The heap rule is local
steps.body: A min-heap only promises heap[i] <= its two children. Siblings are not ordered, so the list is not sorted. That weaker rule is cheap to maintain, and it is enough to guarantee the smallest item is always at heap[0], readable in O(1).

steps.title: heappush: add at the end, sift up
steps.body: heappush(h, 0) on [1, 2, 8, 5, 3] appends 0 at index 5. Its parent is index 2 (value 8), and 0 < 8, so they swap. At index 2 the parent is index 0 (value 1), 0 < 1, swap again. Now 0 is the root: [0, 2, 1, 5, 3, 8]. At most one swap per level, so O(log n).

props.title: heappush(h, 0) then sift up: 0 swaps with 8, then with 1

steps.title: heappop: move the last item to the root, sift down
steps.body: heappop returns h[0]. To fill the hole, the last item is moved to index 0 and pushed down, swapping with its smaller child until both children are larger. Popping [1, 2, 8, 5, 3] returns 1: 3 moves to the root, swaps with the smaller child 2, and the heap becomes [2, 3, 8, 5]. Again O(log n).

props.title: After moving 3 to the root: swap with smaller child 2

steps.title: heapify builds a heap in O(n)
steps.body: heapify does not push items one by one. It sifts down every parent from the last one ((n//2)-1) back to the root. For [5, 3, 8, 1, 2]: 3 swaps with 1, then 5 swaps with 1 and then with 2, giving [1, 2, 8, 3, 5]. Most nodes are near the bottom and move very little, so the total is O(n).

steps.title: Max-heap by negation
steps.body: heapq is only a min-heap. To get the largest first, push -value and negate again when you pop: pushing 3, 1, 4, 1, 5 as negatives puts -5 at the root, and -heappop(h) gives 5. Tuples like (priority, item) work too, because tuples compare element by element.

under_the_hood.takeaway: A heap gives you the minimum in O(1) and insert/remove in O(log n) using nothing but index arithmetic on a list. That is the engine behind priority queues and Dijkstra.
